☆ Tactix: Towards a Programmable Strategy Interface for Flexible SAT Solving
Haoze Wu, André Schidler, Armin Biere, Nina Narodytska
Modern SAT solvers combine a rich repertoire of proof rules with sophisticated strategies that determine when and how to apply them. Often, the internal implementations are tightly coupled to particular strategies, making it inconvenient to define new strategies without changing solver internals. We present Tactix, a proof-producing sequential CDCL solver that incorporates a wide range of techniques in state-of-the-art solvers with a clean separation of proof rules from solving strategies. This separation enables a public interface through which users can invoke particular techniques, observe their effects, and program a wide range of solving strategies. The default strategy of Tactix is programmable over this interface and outperforms state-of-the-art solvers on benchmarks from the 2024--2026 SAT Competitions. We also use the interface to develop novel strategies tailored to challenging benchmarks from two application domains, which led to performance gains over strong baselines. We intend Tactix to serve as an infrastructure for designing and evaluating novel solving strategies. Finally, we also present a self-study of the AI-assisted development process behind Tactix.
♻ ☆ Cyclic Graphs and Memoization in Pure $λ$-Calculus
Bo Yang
Purely functional programming makes immutability and non-strict evaluation its defaults; we push further, making interning and memoization the defaults of computation. In prior operational semantics for the pure $λ$-calculus, representing and transforming cyclic and infinite data requires an added recursion construct, a $\texttt{letrec}$, a $μ$-binder, or a built-in $Y$ for graph reduction, and sharing the repeated work of a memoized or dynamic-programming function requires an impure cache. We show that no extension is needed. We apply tabling, the standard method for solving a least-fixpoint equation, to weak-head reduction; this defines a new operational semantics for the pure $λ$-calculus that keeps each term's standard lazy meaning. A term that reaches finitely many distinct states, each solved in finitely many steps, comes out as a finite graph, possibly cyclic; the calculus stays pure, and the graph is faithful and independent of reduction order. We implemented this operational semantics as a $λ$-calculus interpreter. It does dynamic programming automatically, sharing repeated subproblems with no memoization table. It creates and transforms cyclic graphs with no added recursion construct. And it decides in finite time that some terms have no weak head normal form, returning $\bot$ for $Ω$. What the evaluator returns is a graph, so the $λ$-calculus becomes a DSL for graph computation: the memo table of dynamic programming, the transposition table of game search, and the derived-fact table of Datalog reachability and points-to analysis are all tabling on state identity, and none of them is written by hand. Compilation is one more such problem: we write a bootstrap compiler that compiles its own source, all as a pure $λ$-term.
♻ ☆ Formalizing a Many-Sorted Hybrid Polyadic Modal Logic in Lean
Alexandru Oltean, Bogdan Macovei, Ioana Leuştean
We present a Lean formalization of a general hybrid modal logic with many-sorted signatures and polyadic modal operators. The system borrows ideas from both algebraic specification and dynamic logics, and is designed to serve as a uniform axiomatic foundation for specifying and verifying programming languages and security protocols. We expose a DSL for users to define languages and protocols as many-sorted signatures, specify the relevant domain-specific axioms, and reason about program executions or protocol runs. We provide a machine-checked proof of its soundness theorem and showcase the framework's versatility through several applications: an imperative programming language for code verification, a BAN logic and an epistemic logic used for security protocols, and the modal system S5. We have designed our formalization to be intrinsically sorted, that is, well-sorted formulas in the base language are well-typed terms in Lean. Thanks to intrinsic sorting, all domain specific applications can be easily embedded in our framework via the DSL, at no additional syntactic overhead required for the user to prove. All code presented in this paper is openly accessible in the following repository: https://github.com/alexoltean61/msphml-lean
♻ ☆ A Dichotomy Theorem for Homomorphism Problems on Automatic Structures
Antoine Cuvelier, Rémi Morvan
The field of constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs) studies homomorphism problems between relational structures where the target structure is fixed. Classifying the complexity of these problems has been a central quest of the field, notably when both sides are finite structures. In this paper, we study the generalization where the input is an automatic structure---potentially infinite, but describable by finite automata. We prove a striking dichotomy: homomorphism problems over automatic structures are either decidable in non-deterministic logarithmic space (NL), or undecidable. We show that structures for which the problem is decidable are exactly those with finite duality, which is a classical property of target structures asserting that the existence of a homomorphism into them can be characterized by the absence of a finite set of obstructions in the source structure. Notably, this property precisely characterizes target structures whose homomorphism problem is definable in first-order logic, which is well-known to be decidable over automatic structures. We also consider a natural variant of the problem. While automatic structures are finitely describable, homomorphisms from them into finite structures need not be. This leads to the notion of "regular homomorphism", where the homomorphism itself must be describable by finite automata. Remarkably, we prove that this variant exhibits the same dichotomy, with the same characterization for decidability.
♻ ☆ The Myhill isomorphism theorem does not generalize much
Cécilia Pradic
The Myhill isomorphism is a variant of the Cantor-Bernstein theorem. It states that, from two injections that reduce two subsets of $\mathbb{N}$ to one another, there exists a bijection $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ that preserves them. This theorem can be proven constructively. We investigate to which extent the theorem can be extended to infinite sets other than $\mathbb{N}$. We show that, assuming Markov's principle, the theorem can be extended to the conatural numbers $\mathbb{N}_{\infty}$ provided that we only require that bicomplemented sets are preserved by the bijection. This restriction is essential. Otherwise, the picture is overall negative: among other things, it is impossible to extend that result to either $2 \times \mathbb{N}_{\infty}$, $\mathbb{N} + \mathbb{N}_{\infty}$, $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}_{\infty}$, $\mathbb{N}_{\infty}^2$, $2^{\mathbb{N}}$ or $\mathbb{N}^{\mathbb{N}}$.

♻ ☆ Terminal Coalgebras in Countably Many Steps
Jiří Adámek, Stefan Milius, Lawrence S. Moss
We present a collection of results that imply that an endofunctor on a category has a terminal coalgebra obtainable as a countable limit of its terminal-coalgebra chain. This holds for finitary endofunctors on locally finitely presentable categories under conditions on both the functor and the category. We adapt finiteness arguments that were originally advanced by Worrell concerning terminal coalgebras for finitary set functors. Examples include the categories of sets, posets, vector spaces, graphs, nominal sets, and presheaves on finite sets. Worrell also described, without proof, the terminal-coalgebra chain of the finite power-set functor. We provide a detailed proof following his ideas. We then turn to polynomial endofunctors on the categories of Hausdorff topological spaces and metric spaces. The Vietoris space of compact subsets yields an endofunctor $\mathscr{V}$ on the category of Hausdorff spaces. Vietoris polynomial endofunctors are built from $ \mathscr{V}$, the identity and constant functors by forming products, coproducts and compositions. Their terminal coalgebras are obtained in $ω$ steps. We then turn to the class of Hausdorff polynomial functors on the category of metric spaces, which is analogous but uses in lieu of $\mathscr{V}$ the Hausdorff functor $\mathcal{H}$. We prove they have terminal coalgebras obtained in $ω+ ω$ steps. Finally, we show that every finitary endofunctor on the category of vector spaces over a fixed field again has a terminal coalgebra obtained in $ω+ω$ steps.

Social and Information Networks
☆ Strategic Origins of Network Structure
Christoph Riedl, Rory Smead
The structure and dynamics of complex networks are intimately linked. Despite immense progress in statistically characterizing these systems, a generalized mechanistic framework explaining why specific mesoscale structures emerge remains elusive. Here we introduce the game-graph equilibrium, the stable rest point of a payoff-driven partner-choice dynamic, analogous to a Nash equilibrium. This reveals network structure as the fossilized record of strategic interaction. We prove analytically that two-type games have exactly four network topologies, which are their exhaustive thermodynamic phases: assortative, disassortative, and two core-peripheries. This result generalizes to $K^K$ topological classes for $K$-type interactions. Furthermore, four distinct Nash equilibria produce core-periphery topologies, yet their payoffs reveal whether the underlying dynamic is cooperative or exploitative. To recover the generating dynamics from observed networks, we develop mechanistic inference by constraining a block model to lie on a low-dimensional, game-theoretic manifold. Applied to real-world networks, the model yields interpretable quantities, distinguishes states that look identical to conventional methods, predicts network topologies it has never seen without retraining, and controls its own complexity without hand-tuned penalties. Networks such as international trade are well described by the model despite the hard constraint, suggesting that real-world systems are organized by payoff-driven partner choice. Our framework resolves a foundational ambiguity by offering a precise, mechanistic definition of communities: strategic equivalence.
☆ YouTube Clips and Broad but Shallow Attention to Candidates: Evidence from the 2024 Tokyo Gubernatorial Election
Yoshito Miwa, Kazutoshi Sasahara
Video-sharing platforms and social media have gained influence in election campaigns, and third-party edited videos (called kirinuki in Japanese; hereafter, "clip videos") in particular have attracted attention. In Japan, Shinji Ishimaru, previously unknown nationally, finished second in the 2024 Tokyo gubernatorial election, a result widely attributed to his popularity on YouTube. Focusing on this case, we analyzed 44,331 YouTube videos relating to the nine leading candidates, posted between July 5, 2020, and July 7, 2024. Using cumulative views and engagement data as of June 25, 2025, we examined the relationship between clip videos and the attention candidates received. Regression analyses with standard errors clustered by channel showed that Ishimaru, the most watched candidate, did not draw the most active engagement. Videos mentioning Ishimaru received about 36% fewer likes and 41% fewer comments at the same number of views, whereas some candidates with fewer views recorded higher engagement rates. Clip videos were associated with this breadth of attention. They received about 1.8 times more views but 26% fewer comments at the same number of views, and mentions of Ishimaru were associated with about 2.6 times more views among non-clip videos. The interaction between the two, however, was not significant, and understanding the prominence of Ishimaru's cumulative views requires considering both the number of clip videos about him and the views per video. These results suggest that the spread of attention through clip videos may have functioned as a broad but shallow pathway, distinct from the formation of committed support.
♻ ☆ Monte Carlo Experiments of Network Effects in Randomized Controlled Trials
Márton Trencséni
This paper studies Monte Carlo simulations of content production in Randomized Controlled Trials on social networks modeled as random Watts-Strogatz graphs. Because treatment nodes are surrounded by control nodes, they do not receive the network boost they would receive if the entire network were treated, and part of their boost leaks into control. As a result, the treatment versus control lift underestimates the effect of a full graph-wide rollout. Clustering the treatment group reduces this underestimate, while its size does not depend on the size of the treatment group. These mechanisms appear as seven effects, each captured by a metric: the network effect, spillover effect, experiment dampening effect, intrinsic dampening effect, clustering effect, degree distribution effect and the experiment size effect.

♻ ☆ The Effect of Expertise Signaling when Sharing Medical Information in Opinion Dynamics
Moyi Li, Chuqiao Yan, Jesus Jair Reyes Gutierrez, Aleksandra Urman, Stefania Ionescu
Social media heavily influences health decisions, yet few opinion dynamics models account for how information is delivered. This work investigates how signaling source expertise shapes trust and long-term opinion formation. Through an online experiment, we find that adding a professional title to the sender's display name significantly increases a post's perceived credibility. Incorporating these findings to create a data-driven opinion dynamics model, we prove that (1) connecting users through some paths to an expert guarantees consensus with experts' opinion, while (2) higher rates of expertise signaling accelerate reaching consensus. Simulations show that (3) convincing even 20% of users to signal their title reduces consensus time to nearly one-third in Erdos-Renyi networks and (4) higher title adoption brings average opinion much closer to that of experts in scale-free and real-world networks. Altogether, our work highlights expertise signaling as a viable intervention to promote validated medical information online.

Computers and Society
☆ Source Attribution and Audience Uptake in Digital Witnessing: Evidence from a Chinese Diaspora Account on X
Huiqian Lai, Runze Ding
Digital-witnessing research explains how citizen testimony becomes publicly visible. Less is known about audience uptake after publication and whether the attributed source corresponds to the form of response. This study analyzes 47,635 posts (April 2022 to May 2026) from Teacher Li Is Not Your Teacher, a diaspora-based account that curates and publishes reports and testimony from inside China for transnational audiences. Among 25,093 witness-relevant posts, 3,601 explicitly attribute their material to ordinary submitters. These posts receive more replies than other witness-relevant posts across adjusted analyses and show a more reply-oriented profile. The primary doubly robust retweet estimate is near zero. Among audited replies to November 2022 user-submitted posts, 91.4% substantively engage the focal material. The pattern is consistent with ordinary-person source attribution presenting testimony as situated and open to public response. The study extends digital witnessing beyond visibility by separating redistribution from the public response that gathers around testimony.

☆ How exposed is work to robotics? Occupational, industry, and geographic measures
Sebastian Sartor, Robert Seamans, Neil Thompson
Exposure indices that map technical capabilities onto occupational abilities have become a standard tool for anticipating how AI may reshape work, but existing measures either cover software AI or proxy robotics through patents and installation data that reflect the industrial robots of past decades. We construct the first abilities-based exposure measures for robotics and physical AI, and the first to span occupations, industries, and geographies. Following the framework of Felten et al. (2018, 2021), we build a robotics capability taxonomy of 16 capabilities in eight domains from 78 academic, industry, and standards sources, use a large language model to score the relatedness of each capability to the 52 ONET work abilities, and aggregate to Robotics Occupational Exposure (ROE) for 774 occupations, Robotics Industry Exposure (RIE) for 250 NAICS industries, and county-level Robotics Geographic Exposure (RGE). We find that robotics exposure concentrates in physically intensive work such as construction, farming, transportation, and production, and in industries such as logging, mining, trucking, and warehousing. Unlike generative-AI exposure, ROE is higher in occupations with lower wages, lower education requirements, and less creative-ability content. Physical collaboration and assistance, terrain-based locomotion, grasping and handling, and task and functional reasoning move the exposure ranking most, yet no single capability carries the index. Because the measures capture technical relatedness rather than readiness, cost, or adoption, they should be read as an upper bound on where physical automation could affect work.
☆ Desirability Confirmation: Relational Sycophancy in AI Intimate Roleplay
Huiqian Lai, Runze Ding
Research on LLM sycophancy has largely focused on propositional agreement, in which models echo users' beliefs, preferences, or judgments. Adult intimate roleplay presents a different case because what the user seeks may be preservation of a preferred relational position within a generated scene. Using a controlled prompt-based audit of 2,016 outputs from two open-weight LLMs, we identify four recurrent relational moves: legitimating desire, presenting the user as wanted, preserving non-rejection while communicating limits, and keeping intimacy available within fantasy or roleplay frames. Bringing the sycophancy literature into dialogue with sexual script theory, we conceptualize this configuration as desirability confirmation, an output-level pattern that captures how user-pleasing can operate through relational positioning. The findings extend sycophancy research and intimate-AI evaluation beyond binary compliance or refusal by showing how outputs can differ in the ways they communicate boundaries, preserve relational acceptance, and mark intimacy as fictional.

☆ Usability, User Experience, and Acceptability of the Trail Making Test in Virtual Reality in Younger and Older Adults
Panagiotis Kourtesis, Dante O'Connor, Sarah E. MacPherson
Immersive virtual reality (VR) adaptations of neuropsychological tests change how a test operates. Before their scores are interpreted, the individuals they are intended to assess should find them usable, acceptable and tolerable, and for older adults this evidence is usually missing. This study evaluated the experience of the Trail Making Test in Virtual Reality (TMT-VR), a head-gaze adaptation of the Trail Making Test that requires no hand-held controller, in 47 younger (20-38 years) and 44 older adults (64-81 years). After the task, participants rated usability, pragmatic and hedonic user experience, acceptability, and cybersickness. The study had three aims: to compare the two age groups on these ratings; to examine whether the ratings were associated with age group, gaming and technology experience, and whether cybersickness was associated with motion sickness susceptibility; and to examine whether the ratings were related to TMT-VR completion and error-adjusted times. Both groups rated the TMT-VR as highly usable, acceptable and pleasant to use. Older adults gave slightly lower usability and pragmatic ratings, but neither the age-group differences nor the associations with age group or previous experience were statistically significant after correction. Cybersickness was low, with 38 of the 91 participants reporting no symptoms; it did not differ between the age groups and was not associated with motion sickness susceptibility. No correlation between the ratings and TMT-VR performance survived correction. The TMT-VR with head-gaze selection is therefore usable, acceptable and well tolerated by older as well as younger adults. Because the ratings were favourable across the whole range of TMT-VR scores, slower or less accurate performance is unlikely to reflect difficulty with the interface.

☆ Over reliant and underprepared: First responder resilience to disruption of operational technology
James Connor, Courtney Crooks, Ryan Shandler
The Emergency Services Sector (ESS) is responsible for taking life-saving action in the face of extreme crises. To enhance its response capabilities, the sector has spent the last two decades investing in new technology to improve their operational efficiency. This has created significant interdependencies and a culture among first responders of technical overreliance, raising questions about what would occur if those tools were suddenly disrupted. Several works have discussed the potential for terrorism to intentionally target ESS technology as part of a larger kinetic attack. Despite this, the resilience of first responder agencies to technological disruption and their preparedness for such an attack has largely remained unexplored. To bridge this gap, we implemented a novel scenario-based interview methodology involving senior officials from emergency service agencies across the United States. These interviews explored how each agency prepared for a disruption of operational technology and what factors might influence different levels of preparation between them. Participants were asked to describe their responses to a hypothetical scenario modeled after historical cyber-attacks against ESS infrastructure. The results indicate that while ESS agencies are prepared for short-term technological disruptions, they are likely to struggle with long-term or hybrid incidents. The data further revealed that agencies often lack dedicated expertise in cybersecurity, technology, and emergency management that could otherwise elevate resilience to interruptions of operational technology. These findings emphasize the need for investment in redundant analog systems, increased training for frontline personnel, and a focused effort against loss of specialized technical expertise among ESS agencies.

☆ Bad Diagnosis: Analyzing Consent and Data Collection Practices of Mobile Medical Apps
Ethan Myers, Lorenzo De Carli, Shantanu Sharma, Ritwik Banerjee, Joel Reardon, Indrakshi Ray
Mobile health (mHealth) apps collect personally-identifiable information while handling uniquely sensitive medical data, ranging from mental health records to real-time glucose or heart rate monitoring -- yet they remain poorly understood at scale. We present the first comprehensive analysis of consent and data collection practices across 10,000+ mHealth apps on the Google Play Store, combining static analysis and privacy policy examination. We develop a rigorous operational definition to distinguish health apps from general wellness programs, and design a measurement framework to detect misuse of permissions and violations of consent. Our analyses reveal a troubling ecosystem: 69.15% of apps request at least one permission unrelated to their stated purpose, with over 52.9% apps requesting location data, and 50.5% and 34.9% apps requesting camera and microphone access, respectively -- despite no functional justification based on app descriptions and stated purposes. Most alarmingly, nearly 93% of apps fail to provide users with a consent form, directly violating regulatory requirements such as GDPR; and even among the remaining 7%, 1 in 14 demonstrate a gap between the obtained consent and collection of personally identifiable information. These findings demonstrate an urgent need for stronger enforcement of privacy regulations in mHealth apps. We plan to release our dataset and measurement tools for continued monitoring of this critical space.
☆ A Large Language Model LLM Approach to COVID-19 Fake News Detection
Muhammad Arif, Samah Fodeh-Jarad, Elyas Irankhah, Uroosa Fatima, Lama Ayash, Sreeraj Ramachandran
Text classification is a widely studied problem in information retrieval and data mining, with applications ranging from healthcare diagnosis to the detection of COVID-19-related fake news. Social media platforms generate vast volumes of user-generated text, and the rapid spread of misinformation during the pandemic has made automated fake news detection an important task. In this study, we apply pretrained transformer-based transfer learning (TL) models and large language models (LLMs), namely BERT-base, ALBERT-base, XLM-RoBERTa-base, DistilBERT, GPT-2, XLNet, and T5, to the COVID-19 English Tweets dataset, which contains 6,420 tweets labeled as real or fake. To further improve performance, we apply six late-fusion optimization techniques: weighted fusion, particle swarm optimization (PSO) fusion, the Nelder-Mead algorithm, Powell's method, the Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno (BFGS) algorithm, and trust-region constrained optimization. Models are evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score, and confusion-matrix heatmaps are used to visualize the predictions of each model. GPT-2 achieved the best performance, with an accuracy of 0.9631, precision of 0.9612, recall of 0.9610, and F1-score of 0.9600, while Nelder-Mead fusion achieved the best result among the fusion methods with an accuracy of 0.9610. These results highlight the value of LLMs for COVID-19 fake news detection. We conclude by outlining future directions, including multiclass classification, multilingual datasets, and real-time social media streams.

☆ Bridging the Language Gap in Scholarly Data II: Enhancing Gender Inference for Chinese Names
Lisette Espín-Noboa, Mingrong She, Ana Maria Jaramillo, Liuhuaying Yang
Perceived gender inference from names is important for inclusive scientometrics research, yet existing methods perform poorly on non-Western scholars. We address this gap for Chinese names, which appear in two forms, Hanzi and Pinyin, its Romanized form (e.g., Zhang Wei, Li Na). In international bibliographic records, names are often available only in Pinyin. However, a single pinyin name can correspond to multiple distinct hanzi characters with different gender associations, so gender inference from Pinyin alone is intrinsically ambiguous. To address this, we first develop two hanzi models, a regression model that produces a continuous gender score from 0 (male) to 1 (female), and a classification model that outputs one of three labels (\em{male}, \em{neutral}, \em{female}). We train them on a sample of hanzi names from Chinese-language physics publications, rated by 11 native Chinese speakers. On this sample, the models achieve an RMSE of $0.09$ and an R$^2$ of $0.85$ (regression), and macro-AUC of $0.97$ and a Cohen's $κ$ of $0.81$ (classification), demonstrating high performance that is robust to class imbalance. For pinyin names, we propose a pipeline that aggregates hanzi predictions via transliteration and frequency weighting, together with an ambiguity score that flags names whose gender cannot be resolved from Pinyin alone. Benchmarked against three off-the-shelf tools (Namsor, GPT, and Claude), our models achieve the highest agreement with human annotations for both gender scores and gender labels, in both scripts. Applied to an independent sample of Chinese-named authors in APS journals, our models assign a gender to every name, whereas existing Pinyin-based methods leave between 20\% and 100\% of names unclassified. These findings demonstrate the importance of hanzi-level information for reliable gender inference of Chinese names. Code and data are publicly available.

☆ Water-Energy-Data nexus reveals sustainability gaps and priorities for AI infrastructure
Jincheng Huang, Guoan Xiao, Xin Lan, Caichun Yin, Zhimeng Jiang, Yue Cui, Jianguo Liu
The rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI) depends on interconnected water, energy, and data systems spanning infrastructure life cycles and diverse geographies, with the potential to intensify water and energy insecurity, exacerbate social inequities and lead to cascading sustainability issues globally. Yet assessments commonly examine them separately, limiting our understanding of where resource pressures arise, how they are transferred across space, and who bears their consequences. To address these challenges, we established a water-energy-data (WED) nexus framework that captures the spatial and life-cycle dependencies of AI infrastructure, and use large language models to synthesize 12,825 water- or energy-related studies across four resource-intensive AI infrastructure activities: mineral extraction, semiconductor manufacturing, data center operation and electronic-waste processing. The evidence map identifies a mismatch between the interconnected activities supporting AI infrastructure and boundaries used to assess them. Researchers assess operational energy more than water use and other indirect demands, while interactions across locations and life-cycle activities remain understudied. These gaps obscure how resource demands shift among infrastructure nodes and regions, and how data-enabled benefits compare with their underlying costs. The WED nexus provides a foundation for integrated assessment of spatially metacoupled systems, while the evidence map can inform priorities for managing the sustainability implications of the AI boom.

We introduce GCAM-Gym, a Gymnasium-compatible environment that supports full-policy evaluation and stepwise control through a common interface and exposes the components of the policy objective. ★ Evaluating Predictor-Corrector Dependence in Hard-Constrained Climate Emulators
Tianyu Zhang, Xinyu Wang, Zhenghan Tai, Xiao-Wen Chang, Yoshua Bengio
Climate emulators often enforce physical constraints by correcting each state predicted by a neural network, but evaluating only the corrected forecast conflates predictor skill with the effect of the correction. We introduce an evaluation framework that separates these contributions by comparing corrected forecasts, pre-correction predictions along corrected trajectories, and autonomous rollouts with correction disabled. We further cross correction during training and inference to distinguish its immediate effect from how it shapes the learned predictor, and use matched nonphysical controls to test whether improvements are specific to the physical correction. In ACE2, correction substantially improves physical consistency. In a three-seed ACE2 pilot, models trained with correction produce less accurate uncorrected precipitation forecasts at short horizons than models trained without correction, but more accurate forecasts at 10 and 30 days. This contradicts our preregistered hypothesis that the deficit would grow with forecast horizon. In a separate nine-seed experiment, directly supervising the uncorrected output reverses its precipitation forecast deficit at 72 hours while maintaining the accuracy of corrected forecasts at 24 hours. In ConCerNet's heat-equation system, projection-trained models have higher uncorrected trajectory-based vector-field RMSE than models trained without projection, while restoring the physical projection recovers accuracy far more effectively than a matched nonphysical control. Together, these results show that hard corrections can reshape the predictors trained alongside them, creating dependencies that are not visible from corrected forecasts alone. Hard-constrained emulators should therefore be evaluated by separately measuring predictor accuracy, correction effects, and their interaction during training.

☆ TRACE: Governing AI-Assisted Research with Principles from Computer Science
Amirhossein Zohrehvand, Aldona Kapačinskaitė
Artificial intelligence (AI) makes it easier than ever to produce research outputs. The pressing question is how researchers should organize their work with this technology. The question is not new: software engineering and security research have long studied how teams of people and machines keep control of a shared body of work with many contributors. We distil principles from the practices these literatures report and transpose them to AI-assisted research. The principles form TRACE: Track records, Review against sources, Accept independently, Control transitions, and Evaluate corrections. Together, the five principles give researchers a common basis for remaining in control while integrating AI into their workflows. By bounding units of work and attending to how each is shaped, they help researchers pace AI-assisted work to human attention rather than to the speed at which AI produces content. We also introduce TRACE-OS, an open source operating system for AI-assisted research projects. It puts the principles into practice through shared instructions, tools, and records that fit researchers' existing workflows. The shared standard can contribute to building trust, which allows teams to delegate and realize the productivity that AI promises. More broadly, we aim to open a conversation about the governing principles through which the research community can benefit from AI.

☆ Regulating for an AI Commons: Adopting, sustaining, and defending people-first innovation trajectories
Abhineet Nayyar, Mallory Knodel, Kimberlee Weatherall, Gunn Jiravuttipong
Technological principles of openness, interoperability, and decentralization are integral to building an AI economy that is accountable to the public and truly responsive to local needs and constraints. However, Big Tech's firm control over essential elements of the stack (such as chips, cloud, models, data, and talent) limits valuable alternatives from reaching the scale necessary for sustained growth. Worse still, hyperscalers continue to enclose and extract value from publicly funded and volunteer-driven technologies without adequately distributing these returns. We see consolidated power within a few entities and "enshittification" of once-transformative innovations. Embedding ethical micro-level tools (like open data repositories or small-language models) into workflows is promising, but without a consistent innovation strategy, they also often end up perpetuating and being appropriated by the same exploitative trajectories. Instead, this whitepaper outlines a three-pillared holistic and intentional policy approach that i) actively pushes for the adoption of cooperative technologies in existing and emerging systems, ii) sets up collective institutional structures to sustain and maintain them in the long-term, and iii) introduces regulatory proposals that limit private entities from disempowering them through uncontrolled enclosure and extraction. Through desk research and purpose-specific case studies, we argue for the importance of such an approach in the Global South, where structural constraints around infrastructure, financing, and policy governance make it difficult for AI commons and cooperative AI tools to emerge and survive. The paper concludes with key open questions for campaigners, policy advocates, researchers, and grassroots organizers to consider and explore while working towards peoples' solidarity within and between Global South countries.
☆ Can AI interview? Comparing AI-led to Human-led Chat Interviews
Semra Guven, Tobias Gårdhus, Andreas Bjerre-Nielsen, Anna Rogers, Hjalmar Bang Carlsen
Large language model chatbots have been proposed as AI-interviewers for collecting qualitative interview data at scale, potentially bridging social science's longstanding divide between the breadth of surveys and the depth of qualitative interviews. This paper provides the first direct empirical comparison of data quality in AI-led and human-led interviews. In a randomized experiment (N = 41), university students were interviewed via synchronous text chat by either trained non-expert interviewers or a locally hosted AI system; we evaluate exposure, specificity, and relevance. Median interview duration was similar across conditions, but AI-interviewers asked more than twice as many questions per interview and elicited roughly 65 percent more respondent text per interview. Per-question responses were longer with human interviewers, though not after multiple-testing correction; only AI-condition participants skipped questions. Responses were almost uniformly on-topic in both conditions; for specificity we detect no difference, but the design cannot exclude one of up to three quarters of a point. These results were obtained with a small, locally hosted open-weight model (7B parameters), which addresses concerns about data security, GDPR compliance, and scientific reproducibility. Our findings support the viability of AI-interviewing for large-N qualitative data collection.

☆ Same Person, Different Advice: Auditing LLM Financial Advice with Repeated Risk-Tolerance Responses
Soovadeep Bakshi, Apurba Bose, Aishwarya Bose, Sandip Nandi
AI financial advisers set a client's stock allocation largely from one stated-risk question, yet people do not answer it the same way twice: in a national US panel, 41% of households chose a different answer two years later, and in a laboratory retest a third of people moved two or more points on a 0-10 scale after six months. Seven large language models from five providers gave one-turn allocation advice for 800 real household profiles in which only the risk answer changed. The recommended stock share moved by 10 to 16 percentage points on average, and by 24 to 35 when the answer changed, against 0.6 to 4.2 points for the same prompt asked twice; in the laboratory retest the rating alone moved advice by 11 to 18 points. Without any note, the models respond to the answer about as strongly as when told that it is very reliable (less so for the two Claude models). If that instructed response is how each model maps attitude to advice, discounting the answer for its measured reliability, as classical test theory prescribes, would cut the swings by a factor of 2.4 to 3.3. The swing is largest for clients under 40. A note that the answer is noisy steadies some models, but shifts their weight to the client's age and pulls cautious clients towards a generic middle allocation: clients unwilling to take any risk are advised 22% stocks instead of 4%. Three extra money questions reduce the swing for some models, with no statistically detectable change relative to how much advice differs across people. In a scripted test, one clarifying question removes nearly all of the swing from an answer the client then corrects (33.5 points to 1.9 on average) while keeping the response to a change the client confirms. We argue that same-person retest audits should be a standard check for AI advisers, and that what to do with an unreliable answer is a question of client autonomy as well as of statistics.

☆ Causal Value Attribution of Marketing Labels in LLM-Generated Ads: A Deconfounder Approach
Danhong You, Wei Jiang, Zhiqiang, Zheng
As AI-generated content becomes commoditized, economic value increasingly shifts from final artifacts to the upstream expertise used to specify inputs that steer LLM generation. Yet organizations lack methods for valuing this expertise and identifying which individual skills or configurations causally improve performance. This study examines generative marketing, where structured expert labels serve as skill primitives conditioning LLM-generated advertisements. Estimating their causal effects is difficult because outcomes reflect stochastic LLM mediation, high-dimensional label interactions, and multimodal confounding. This study proposes D-VAE (Deconfounder Variational Autoencoder), a counterfactual-inference framework integrating a multi-treatment deconfounder with causal representation learning. D-VAE recovers causally disentangled expert-labeling logic and derives PAC-based bounds on omitted-variable bias from single-treatment confounders. Applied to 29,177 foundation-makeup ad creatives, D-VAE outperforms state-of-the-art benchmarks. A field experiment shows that recommended configurations increase engagement by 32.7% and perform statistically indistinguishably from human experts, while a simulation study confirms causal attribution under complex confounding and treatment interactions. Overall, the study shifts value assessment from AI-generated products to skills, providing a foundation for pricing and optimizing AI-augmented skill portfolios.

☆ Provable Compliance: A Protocol for Runtime Compliance Evidence and Transaction-Specific Decisioning
Jeremy Blackburn, Tim Hines, Matthew Koepp, Russell Lessard, Jason Patrick
Regulated institutions already perform onboarding, screening, monitoring, and review, but compliance evidence ages, and whether it supports a decision depends on the institution, product, subject, counterparty, transaction, jurisdiction, risk tier, and purpose. A relying party therefore often cannot obtain compact, attributable proof of which evidence, policy, authority, and transaction context were current when a decision was made, a gap that grows as authority is delegated to software agents and scheduled workflows. We describe ChainIT Provable Compliance, the compliance-side layer of the ChainIT Authority Protocol. Each sourced or institution-generated fact is represented as a separate Evidence Assertion VDT with provenance, freshness, confidence, permitted purpose, and privacy classification; a versioned Compliance Policy Profile selects the applicable rules; a Business Rules Engine returns deterministic, reason-coded predicate results; and the organization's configured Workflow Engine composes them into a signed, time-bounded Compliance Decision VDT for one reliance event. The decision contributes a single predicate, Compliance Decision Permits, to session-eligibility and transaction-policy decisions. It never independently authorizes payment: only a final Allow together with an exact transaction digest, atomic capacity reservation, and a single-use execution credential can commit value. The paper specifies point-of-reliance freshness, scoped propagation of evidence changes, decision states, evidence domains (AML, sanctions, PEP, background, identity, and licensing), the U.S. and FATF regulatory context as of August 2026, privacy and disclosure controls, and residual risks.

♻ ☆ Using Agency Law to Tame AI Agents
Deven R. Desai, Mark O. Riedl
Artificial Intelligence (AI) Agents have entered the marketplace. By some estimates, AI Agents, which promise to execute tasks and even take over your computer to do so, present a more than $400 billion market. The potential power of AI Agents has fueled legal scholars' fears that AI Agents will enable rogue commerce, human manipulation, rampant defamation, and infringement of intellectual property rights. These scholars are calling for regulation before AI Agents cause havoc. This Article addresses concerns about AI Agents head-on. The Article leverages the socio-legal issues presented by agency law to identify potential problems. It then asks how computer science can solve those problems rather than trying to take rules for humans and impose them on software. This approach shows that core aspects of modern software engineering, particularly client server architectures, address several of those concerns in ways quite different from---and arguably stronger than---how the law would discipline a human agent.

♻ ☆ Selective Data Expansion for Model Performance
Jahid Hasan, Romila Pradhan
Machine learning systems are increasingly being used in critical decision making such as healthcare, finance, and criminal justice. Concerns around their fairness have resulted in several bias mitigation techniques that emphasize the need for high-quality data to ensure fairer decisions. However, the role of earlier stages of machine learning pipelines in mitigating model bias has not been explored well. In this paper, we focus on the task of acquiring additional labeled data points for training the downstream machine learning model to rapidly improve its fairness. Since not all data points in a data pool are equally beneficial to the task of fairness, we generate an ordering in which data points should be acquired. We present DataSift, a data acquisition framework based on the idea of data valuation that relies on partitioning and multi-armed bandits to determine the most valuable data points to acquire. Over several iterations, DataSift selects a partition and randomly samples a batch of data points from the selected partition, evaluates the benefit of acquiring the batch on model fairness, and updates the utility of partitions depending on the benefit. To further improve the effectiveness and efficiency of evaluating batches, we leverage influence functions that estimate the effect of acquiring a batch without retraining the model. We empirically evaluate DataSift on several real-world and synthetic datasets and show that the fairness of a machine learning model can be significantly improved even while acquiring a few data points.

♻ ☆ Bridging the Gap in the Responsible AI Divides
Bálint Gyevnár, Atoosa Kasirzadeh
Tensions between AI Safety (AIS) and AI Ethics (AIE) have created what we term a "responsible AI divide." This divide has been persistent, and has dominated the public and policy discourse on AI, and increasingly shapes how governments, firms, and researchers define responsible AI, and so which AI risks they prioritize, which they sideline, and which mitigation strategies they ultimately develop and implement. Here, we first introduce categorization with four major conceptual modes of possible engagement with these tensions: radical confrontation, disengagement, compartmentalized coexistence, and critical bridging. Second, we discuss the advantages and disadvantages of the modes of engagement. Third, we empirically analyze a well-curated set of 3555 research papers roughly representing AIS and AIE. Using computational tools and qualitative analyses, we map the research landscapes of AIE and AIS. We observe that there are several shared research problems between AIE and AIS. However, there are also several thematic divides. For example, we find that AIE has long grappled with problems related to injustice incurred by AI and tangible AI harms, whereas AIS has primarily embodied an anticipatory approach focused on mitigating risks from AI capabilities. At the same time, we find significant overlap in core research concerns across AIE and AIS regarding transparency, reproducibility, and inadequate governance mechanisms. Based on our empirical observations, we claim that critical bridging, with a focus on bridging problems, offers one viable, constructive path for advancing responsible AI. We conclude by identifying bridging problems as a foundation for collaborative AI governance, offering concrete recommendations for integrating shared considerations into responsible AI practice, discussing the limitations of critical bridging, and outlining open problems for future research.

♻ ☆ MARTA Reach: Toward an On-Demand Multimodal Transit System in Atlanta
Pascal Van Hentenryck, Connor Riley, Anthony Trasatti, Hongzhao Guan, Tejas Santanam, Jorge A. Huertas, Kevin Dalmeijer, Kari Watkins, Juwon Drake, Samson Baskin
On-Demand Multimodal Transit Systems (ODMTS) adopt a transit-centric model, integrating fixed-route public transit with on-demand shuttles to provide integrated, door-to-door multimodal service. Although simulation studies have demonstrated the theoretical potential of ODMTS, the system has not yet been tested in practice at scale. In collaboration with the transit agency of the Atlanta metropolitan region (MARTA), the authors organized MARTA Reach, a six-month on-demand mobility pilot to explore the practical viability of ODMTS. Reach offered on-demand services across four different zones, connecting each zone to the existing transit network and offering an integrated flat fare. This allowed for testing key system components in real-world conditions. Ridership steadily increased throughout the pilot, suggesting potential for growth if a full ODMTS were implemented. Reach offered a highly valued service with 94% satisfaction rate, and 12.24% of survey respondents indicated they would have driven, ridden with someone, or taken a taxi or ride-hailing service otherwise. The vast majority of Reach trips were multimodal, especially in West Atlanta, where over 70% of morning riders connected to rail. The paper presents a potential path to economic viability and discusses practical challenges encountered during the pilot, along with strategies for future deployments. Following the pilot, MARTA officially adopted MARTA Reach as a long-term component of its transportation services in March 2026. The system-wide on-demand transit service currently serves 12 zones with the integrated flat fare and the organizational structure advocated in the pilot. The adoption decision demonstrates that the insights, system components, and operational lessons documented in this paper translated directly into a larger real-world deployment, providing an opportunity to evaluate ODMTS performance at scale.

In this survey, we examine NLP research papers that explicitly address the relationship between LGBTQIA+ communities and NLP technologies. We systematically review all such papers published in the ACL Anthology up until February 2026 (n=122), to answer the following research questions: (1) What are current research trends? (2) What gaps exist in terms of topics and methods? (3) What areas are open for future work? We find that while the number of papers on queer NLP has grown within the last few years, most papers take a reactive rather than a proactive approach, focusing on shortcomings of existing systems rather than creating new solutions. We also offer an outlook from a queer studies perspective, highlighting understudied topics and blind spots in the harms addressed in NLP papers. Beyond being a roadmap of what has been done, this survey is a call to action for work towards more just and inclusive NLP technologies.

Tobias Holtdirk, Dennis Assenmacher, Arnim Bleier, Claudia Wagner

While recent work has explored the use of large language models (LLMs) for simulating survey responses, most studies focus on the U.S. population and assume relatively favourable data conditions with limited or random missingness. In this work, we investigate whether LLMs can leverage contextual knowledge about socio-demographic and political patterns to predict vote choice in the German population under sampling constraints. We systematically vary both the size and composition of training data, ranging from large representative samples to small, biased convenience samples, and compare zero-shot prompting and supervised fine-tuning against established tabular classifiers such as CatBoost. Our results show that when representative training data are available, fine-tuned LLMs achieve predictive performance comparable to strong tabular baselines and substantially outperform zero-shot prompting. Under small and biased convenience samples, however, fine-tuned LLMs more accurately recover both individual-level vote choice and population-level distributions than zero-shot approaches and often outperform tabular methods. These findings suggest that fine-tuned LLMs can combine sample-specific information with contextual knowledge acquired during pre-training, enabling more robust inference under conditions of sampling bias and missing data.

♻ ☆ Risk Ceilings and Development Deadlines: Pacing AI under Uncertain Safety Productivity
Li Gan
Can a regulator promise both a risk ceiling and a development deadline when safety productivity is unknown? A ceiling below the final model's unprotected hazard requires a minimum stock of safety knowledge, so both promises hold only if weak research can be ruled out. Learning first and then replaying development, with spare compute in safety, comes close to that minimum. In a calibration with only state risk, constant safety yield, and full knowledge transfer, it needs only 3.3 percent more productivity than the necessary bound. Customer services pay for the guarantee. Rules that fix compute allocation fix dates, not risk.

These findings indicate that demographic bias in T2I face generation is both pervasive and shaped by emotional conditioning. They underscore the need for intersectional, emotion-conditioned, and multilingual demographic audits as part of standard pre-deployment evaluation practices.

Overall, we show that AI is not only prominent in everyday LLM advice, but also receives systematically inflated quantitative estimates compared to non-AI cases, even against its closest disciplinary neighbors, raising concerns for high-stakes decision support.

♻ ☆ CABAL: Multi-Agent Simulacra for Tracing the Effects of Collusive Bidding in Peer Review

Recent reports during the AAAI-27 review cycle highlight the risk of reviewers coordinating bids for reciprocal assignment advantage. Prior work treats bidding, reviewer assignment, and review manipulation as separate stages, leaving the lifecycle effects of collusive bidding unclear. Real-world analysis is further constrained by typically unobservable collusive intent and the lack of counterfactuals for the same conference. Motivated by this gap, we introduce \alg, an end-to-end multi-agent simulacra framework for studying reviewer assignment integrity by holding the conference environment fixed and configuring LLM-driven reviewer agents with honest or collusive policies. We further develop an affinity-guided collusive bidding strategy that uses mutual reviewer-paper affinities to construct collusion rings and select target papers, producing expertise-consistent rather than arbitrarily targeted attacks. Controlled experiments show that collusive bidding more than doubles target-paper capture and that assigned colluders score target papers about two points higher than honest co-reviewers, while conference-wide effects remain comparatively modest. Evaluated bid-phase detectors provide only limited evidence of collusion: in a fixed-triplet detector stress test, native positive-bid graphs are confounded by benign affinity, while a Very-High-only diagnostic view enables precise but low-coverage local recovery.

Mirko Degli Esposti
Synthetic populations of eleven Italian municipalities (1,814,317 individuals in 887,937 households) generated from published aggregates alone: ISTAT census and register tables, census-section counts, the national civic-address register, public-use survey microdata, and six municipal open-data portals, every source certified in a registry with licence, fingerprint and declared affordances. Four rings give every attribute a declared place: a maximum-entropy joint model of up to nine demographic attributes; whole-vector donation of twenty-three attitudinal and health variables from survey respondents; placement to census section, single year of age and address; and households constrained by the census size distribution per section. Every downstream layer (detailed titles, work, names, biographies) is a declared derivation adding no information. The pipeline is deterministic to the byte: regenerating all eleven municipalities from the tagged commit reproduces every file of every ring bit for bit, in 33 minutes on one workstation. Populations are released in a public regime enforced in the data (no names, no addresses, coordinates randomised within census section), browsable in Animarium, a dependency-free web viewer where every number carries its comparison and every view is a citable URL, and downloadable as an open dataset. The report documents the architecture, the sources and their certification, the reproducibility and quality measurements at the release tag, the viewer, and the narrative layer that renders records into personas for LLM-driven simulation, with the platform's controllability demonstrated in companion experiments, and validation explicitly out of scope.

We propose a Runtime Assurance Contract (RAC), a policy-level formal schema binding autonomy boundaries, component eligibility, evidence state, transition policy, human-review capacity, and non-compensatory gates. Under RAC, soft metrics may inform routing, whereas a failed or unknown mandatory gate forces retry, switch, escalation, deferral, or stop; aggregate performance cannot authorize action. We define the contract, an evidence record, a permission rule, and five invariants. A deterministic failure-injection study in agentic coding evaluates 174 cases, each a distinct mechanism, under a gate conjunction, a score-only rule, and a restricted protocol baseline. At the published example weights and threshold, the score rule admits 56 of 63 block-required injections and all 24 review-required injections; tuned in hindsight, it matches the conjunction case for case. For positive weights, a positive threshold, binary risk signals, and each signal firing alone on some case, the two rules agree on every case if and only if the threshold does not exceed the smallest weight. On 124 further cases written blind by a model of another vendor, the conjunction itself admits 35 of 79 injections, and so does the tuned score rule: a missing detector is invisible to every decision rule. Eighteen hand-authored traces check version-pinned evidence and review transitions. In a prospective synthetic holdout of 24 episodes, RAC and a separately implemented full stateful baseline both match the labels of two blinded LLM judges. These studies test mechanisms on synthetic cases; they establish neither deployed safety nor cross-domain effectiveness.

♻ ☆ Language Model Goal Selection Differs from Humans' in a Self-Directed Learning Task
Gaia Molinaro, Dave August, Danielle Perszyk, Anne G. E. Collins
Whether in agentic workflows, social studies, or chat settings, large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being asked to replace humans in choosing which goals to pursue, rather than completing predefined tasks. However, the assumption that LLMs accurately reflect human preferences for goal setting remains largely untested. We assess the validity of LLMs as proxies for human goal selection in a controlled, self-directed learning task borrowed from cognitive science. Across five models (GPT-5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Qwen3 32B, and Centaur), we find substantial divergence from human behavior. While people gradually explore and learn to achieve goals with diversity across individuals, most models exploit a single identified solution or show surprisingly low performance, with distinct patterns across models and little variability across instances of the same model. Chain-of-thought reasoning and persona steering provide limited improvements, and our conclusions hold across experimental settings. While they await confirmation in applied settings, these findings highlight the uniqueness of human goal selection and caution against its replacement with current models.

☆ Integer Reachability in Data VASS
Roland Guttenberg, Łukasz Kamiński, Sławomir Lasota
Data Petri nets are an extension of plain Petri nets where, intuitively speaking, tokens carry data values, and transitions may perform equality tests on data values involved. Likewise, data vector addition systems with states (data VASS) are an extension of plain VASS, and equivalent to data Petri nets. The decidability status of the reachability problem in this model is an established and long-standing open question. In this paper we perform a major step towards resolving this question: we show decidability of the integer reachability problem, where the counters can drop below zero. Contrarily to plain VASS, where integer reachability reduces to integer linear programming, the setting of data VASS is significantly more complex, mostly due to the fact that the state spaces are not finite but orbit-finite (like in register automata). Our decision procedure combines an iterative refinement, resembling the KLM decomposition in plain VASS, with a termination argument via a novel way of bounding the number of data values appearing in the refinement. As corollaries, we deduce decidability of a number of decision problems concerning register automata and data Petri nets.

A ring Petri net (weighted circuit, cyclic weighted T-system) consists of a single directed circuit with arbitrary positive arc weights. We show that deciding liveness of ring Petri nets is coNP-complete, and that coNP-hardness holds in the strong sense already for token-conserving rings, in which every transition consumes and produces the same number of tokens. The proof is a short reduction from the covering problem for systems of residue classes (the complement of Simultaneous Incongruences). Together with a known reduction to circuits, it follows that liveness of weighted T-systems (weighted marked graphs, synchronous dataflow graphs) is coNP-complete, and coNP-hard in the strong sense. As a further consequence, the halting problem for chip-firing on simple directed graphs is NP-complete, which answers a question of Farrell and Levine. On 7 October 2026, the problem of liveness was posed to the AI model Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), which found the reduction, also suggesting the application to the chip-firing problem, and wrote a first version of this paper; the human authors checked it and, together with the model, revised it iteratively into the present form.

This work is concerned with describing when the toric model is precise enough to decide whether the trace of a system is contained in an omega-regular language. Our contributions are threefold. (i) We use topological means to generalise a class of toric words by defining noise-robust dynamical systems and their sets of noisy traces. We prove that all noisy traces of a system are almost-periodic, and have the same set of recurrent factors. (ii) We apply the abstract techniques above to concrete sequences obtained as sign descriptions of real algebraic linear recurrence sequences (LRS), and show that the language-membership problem for sign descriptions of LRS with few dominant roots is decidable. (iii) We show that noisy traces of noise-robust dynamical systems are indistinguishable to a prefix-independent omega-regular language, and inclusion is decidable provided the common language of their recurrent factors is recursive. We incidentally obtain properties of prefix-independent omega-regular languages that may be of independent interest.

We describe the admissible set exactly. The two manufacturing rules forbid a finite set of factors, so the sequences they admit form a regular language, recognised by an automaton that tracks the last orientation and the length of its run; balance and the ten per cent rule constrain the Parikh vector and are carried by a dynamic program over automaton state and counters. One table, polynomial in N, counts the admissible sequences without producing them, draws them uniformly, and tells whether a partial sequence can still be completed. We give pseudocode, exact counts for three orientation sets, closed-form ceilings on the composition, and four of the five single-rule entries a published table left uncomputed. At 48 plies, 99.8% of the nodes of a layer-wise search tree checking the rules locally have no admissible completion on eight orientations; the completion test removes them. A one-point crossover that cuts two admissible parents only where they share an automaton state and their child closes the counters returns admissible children by construction.

☆ Finitely Verifiable Segmentation: Decidability for Every Tokenizer with a Finite-State Verifier
Nicklas Nidhögg
A segmentation policy assigns to each byte string at most one segmentation into tokens. Call it finitely verifiable when a finite automaton over marked strings, bytes paired with boundary bits, accepts exactly the policy's own segmentations. The automaton judges a proposed segmentation and need not compute one. The paper shows what that hypothesis buys. Four questions that practice settles by folklore become decidable, whether a window certifies a token boundary, whether the boundary gap is bounded, whether a mask keeps generation completable, and whether two policies are equivalent. The last three specialize limitedness, coaccessibility and the equivalence of single-valued transducers. The first refines the synchronizing cut of code theory, and two more ask whether a certified cut, or the cuts of an inventory, let each piece scan alone. The class sits strictly between the online-scannable policies and those with regular domains, and its inner frontier is Choffrut's and decidable in polynomial time. Markings are length-preserving, so the class is exactly the rational segmentation policies, a normal form rather than a restriction, and what the decisions need is a supplied verifier. The class is closed under the operations pipelines use: composition over a labeled stage, restriction, splitting, and byte-fallback union of literal policies. Each composite inherits the six decisions, and certificates transfer between stages under four laws. Under rational, unifilar, almost surely stopping finite-state sources, each mass of the weighted section is an exact rational, and so is each rate where expected length is positive. Maximal-munch lexing, canonical byte-pair encoding and two-mode WordPiece instantiate the interface, and the munch library implements all six decisions. Every theorem carries an executable check, and every reported statistic is a program's own output.

Across five paired seeds on the REES46 cosmetics-shop dataset, with matched training for all three models, candidate-dependent routing leaves the primary metric, normalized discounted cumulative gain at cutoff ten (NDCG@10), essentially unchanged (mean relative change +0.003%). The candidate-dependent model places more relevant items in its top ten (recall +1.81%) but ranks the first one lower (mean reciprocal rank -1.09%), and most of its new hits land at positions six to ten. Its gains come from queries with at least one target among the user's last 50 events, while queries whose targets all lie outside that window get worse. In this form, candidate-dependent routing trades accuracy at the top of the list for recall further down.

Context-to-LoRA methods encode documents as low-rank parameter updates, allowing language models to answer without retaining the source text in their decoding context. How reliably do these updates preserve facts and support their use under different instructions? Controlled diagnosis of existing context-to-LoRA methods separates fact discrimination, target retention, and response adaptation. Competing sources influence answers, while target-only construction and memory-state optimization improve recovery at fixed update size. Recovering facts also does not ensure that answers follow response instructions. Across 17 tasks, Cache2LoRA improves on existing context-to-LoRA methods and achieves macro F1 of 0.663, approaching full-context in-context learning at 0.671. For 32K documents and 256-token outputs at batch size 16, its decoding throughput is 5.9$\times$ that of full-context ICL. In this paper, we present a controlled audit of how the user's location changes the sources that generative engines cite. We ask 300 questions of ChatGPT with 19 declared locations, and of ChatGPT and Gemini from five network locations, each twice to measure run-to-run noise (31,200 answers). The engines take location from different channels. ChatGPT follows the location an application declares, down to the city: it writes the place into its own searches, and its search backend localizes results even when the queries name no place. It ignores the network. Gemini ignores the declared location and follows the country of the network, changing most of its sources even for questions that do not depend on place. The businesses the answers recommend change with the sources. Thus, visibility in generative search is specific to the user's location, and audits must control both channels.

Humanity's Last Choice describes the idea that the last choice people need to make is which AI system they entrust with the decisions that follow. These systems rely on external sources that content providers can edit through generative engine optimization (GEO) to increase source visibility and influence recommendations. Choosing among these systems therefore requires comparable evidence of how well they carry out user requests when exposed to GEO. Benchmarks have made progress in standardizing tasks, models, and metrics, but they often define their own spaces of GEO strategies and use different editing constraints. These differences can conflate gains from better optimization algorithms with those from greater freedom to edit sources, while making evaluation coverage difficult to compare across benchmarks. We therefore call for a common evaluation standard and propose a meta-taxonomy that describes where sources are edited, how they are edited, and what signals those edits target. Drawing on representative literature, we map existing strategies into a searchable space and outline a protocol for controlled comparisons with explicit coverage reporting. This provides a foundation for common leaderboards that can inform which systems people choose to rely on.

☆ LSNR: Learned Sparse News Recommendations with Attentive User Modeling SIGIR
David Vos, Andrew Yates, Maarten de Rijke
Current learned sparse approaches for recommender systems, such as STAR, represent a user by concatenating their interaction history into a single query string. For news, this creates two bottlenecks: concatenation collapses a user's distinct reading interests into one flat query, and, because news articles are long-form text, concatenating several news articles quickly overruns the context window of the language model used as backbone and forces quality-degrading truncation. To address both bottlenecks, we introduce learned sparse news recommendations (LSNR). LSNR encodes each article independently and constructs a sparse user vector by combining learned, attention-based weighting of the per-article sparse representations with a dense-projected expansion at the user level. Experiments on the MIND and EBNeRD datasets show that LSNR significantly outperforms STAR, with these gains holding even in short-history settings where truncation is not a factor. Compared to state-of-the-art dense recommenders, LSNR is competitive in standard settings and it outperforms them when the user history is short. An ablation of the user encoder confirms that learned attention-based aggregation outperforms simpler pooling alternatives. Beyond effectiveness, an additional advantage of LSNR is that it serves from an index an order of magnitude smaller than an uncompressed dense baseline.

The strongest post-trained model, the 8B model trained with a graded ranking reward, gives the best SID-only ranking and matches strong text-reading LLMs whose prompts are about 20x longer. It ranks above random with no history at all, where a caption-reading reference does not, and it keeps its gains at long histories, where text prompts pass 50k tokens and the caption-reading reference stops improving. In a paired rationale audit, this model argues trade-offs better than that reference but describes items less accurately. The common post-training methods we test thus elicit ranking from SIDs but not faithful item descriptions, which calls for post-training that improves the reasoning itself, not only the ranking it produces.

♻ ☆ Upgrade the Retriever First: What an LLM Call per Chunk Buys in RAG
Bhavik Mangla
Many RAG pipelines pay one LLM call per chunk at indexing time to add titles, summaries, keywords and questions (enrichment) or document context (contextual retrieval, CR). We ask what that call buys over free structure and a better retriever. Our advice: upgrade the retriever first, chunk at headers, and enrich mainly for lexical retrieval. Under a plan made public before any index was built, 7B enrichment beats a free section-path prefix under a hybrid retriever by +5.5 recall points on Qasper; on FreshStack its gain (+2.7) does not survive Holm adjustment. It is equivalent to CR, which sends 5.8-8.7 times the input tokens, and Qasper answer F1 (7B reader) is equivalent for both contrasts. Header-led chunks beat 512-character windows; on FreshStack they lose to overlapping 256-token windows. Under qwen3-embedding and a reranker, the two strongest of eight retrievers (named as secondary before any outcome was computed), the CIs of 7B enrichment against the free prefix fall within the equivalence margins; under BM25 it gains +8.7. Exploratory analyses attribute the hybrid gain to document expansion and to repairing an untuned rank fusion; the free prefix under either strong retriever beats hybrid enrichment by +3.4 to +6.3 points, though the best 120B-indexed configuration leads the best free one by +2.5 on Qasper. Add-ons built on the call do no better than LLM-free controls, and late chunking lowers Qasper recall. We release the plan, harness and per-question results.
comment: 29 pages (8-page main text). v4: confirmatory study with a plan made public before any index was built (951 Qasper and 235 FreshStack questions, eight retrievers). Results of v1-v2 are withdrawn (Appendix P). Code and data: https://github.com/bhavik-mangla/MDKeyChunker
♻ ☆ PANINI-DR: Controlled Deep Research through Generative Semantic Workspaces ICLR 2027
M. Yigit Turali, Shreyas Rajesh, M. Efe Lorasdagi, Chenda Duan, Kartik Sharma, Vwani Roychowdhury
Deep research requires connecting multiple steps of search, reasoning, and computation, with intermediate findings guiding what to investigate next. As investigations grow, agents must maintain research state across model calls and check findings before errors propagate into subsequent work. We introduce PANINI-DR, a multi-agent harness that separates coordination of the overall investigation from the research and verification of individual subquestions. A shared workspace, built on the Generative Semantic Workspace representation, records subquestions, their dependencies, findings, and supporting evidence. Researchers investigate individual subquestions, while a separate verification agent checks proposed answers against those subquestions and their evidence. Verification feedback guides further investigation, and recorded findings inform subsequent assignments. We evaluate PANINI-DR on BrowseComp-Plus, FRAMES, and MoNaCo against seven state-of-the-art deep-research harnesses, all using a shared language-model backbone and frozen corpora. PANINI-DR achieves the strongest average performance across the three benchmarks. On BrowseComp-Plus, it achieves 73.3% accuracy, outperforming the next-best harness by 16.0 points. Its advantage is strongest on hard questions, where it answers nearly twice as many as the next-best harness. Ablations further show that structured planning and persistent state improve performance, as does checking each finding against its cited evidence before it is reused. Because a model can answer correctly from memory alone, we also analyze the evidence retained by each harness. PANINI-DR achieves the highest answer recoverability from saved evidence on all three benchmarks, while complementary claim-support audits show stronger evidence-backed answers. Accounting for this evidence changes how harnesses compare and further strengthens PANINI-DR's advantage.
comment: Under review at ICLR 2027. 37 pages, 1 figure, 22 tables. M. Yigit Turali and Shreyas Rajesh contributed equally. Code: https://github.com/roychowdhuryresearch/panini-dr. Project page: https://roychowdhuryresearch.github.io/PANINI-DR_Project_Page/
♻ ☆ Your Embedding Model is SMARTer Than You Think NeurIPS 2026
Jianrui Zhang, Hyun Jung Lee, Sukanta Ganguly, Tae-Eui Kam, Donghyun Kim, Yong Jae Lee
Multimodal retrieval relies heavily on single-vector retrievers, which compress rich, sequential token sequences into one single global representation. While efficient, they discard fine-grained, local evidence critical for dense retrieval tasks. Multi-vector approaches were introduced as a solution, but they strictly require training and many ignore the necessity of a globally summarizing representation. To address this, we introduce SMART, a framework that unlocks the latent multi-vector capabilities of standard single-vector models. We first observe that gradients from the pooled contrastive objective reach the preceding hidden states, and then show empirically that these states are already organized for cosine-based matching. By applying direct late-interaction over these frozen hidden states during inference, SMART acts as a plug-and-play upgrade that consistently improves performance across diverse modalities, improving even the state-of-the-art models further on MMEB-V2. We also show that lightweight post-training saves time and compute while further improving Visual Document retrieval, allowing a single-vector model to perform competitively with SoTA multi-vector counterparts. SMART targets dense retrieval: its gains concentrate on fine-grained and visual-document tasks, it is on par on global tasks such as classification, and it trades additional per-token index storage for these gains. Ultimately, SMART offers both a highly efficient inference enhancement and a powerful finetuning technique for multimodal retrieval. We open source our code and weights at https://github.com/HanSolo9682/SMART.
comment: NeurIPS 2026
♻ ☆ GenPage: Towards End-to-End Generative Homepage Construction at Netflix RecSys 2026
Lequn Wang, Jiangwei Pan, Fengdi Che, Linas Baltrunas
We present GenPage, an end-to-end generative approach to Netflix homepage construction that replaces the traditional multi-stage recommender stack with a single transformer. GenPage treats the user and request context as a prompt and autoregressively generates the entire structured, multi-row homepage as the response. We adapt the LLM training recipe: pretraining on production pages, followed by post-training via weighted binary classification (WBC) or reinforcement learning (RL). For industry-scale deployment, we introduce techniques addressing cold start, model freshness, business-rule enforcement, and serving efficiency. In online A/B tests against a mature, highly optimized production homepage recommender, GenPage delivered a substantial lift on the core user engagement metric we use for launch decisions, while reducing end-to-end serving latency by 20%. Offline, two findings stand out: enriching the prompt yields a larger improvement than scaling model capacity in our current regime, and RL post-training increases homepage diversity even though diversity is not part of the objective.
