♻ ☆ UniRec: Cross-stage Multi-Task Fusion with Preference Optimization for Cascaded Recommender Systems
Lingyuan Kong, Jiaqi Cui, Fanjiao Zeng, Congqi Wang, Yu Li, Yuan Cheng, Jingxin Liu, Xiaoshuang Chen, Kaiqiao Zhan
Industrial recommender systems use cascaded stages with different candidate spaces, data distributions, and latency constraints. Independently optimizing their multi-task fusion (MTF) modules can cause cross-stage preference inconsistency, while existing cross-stage methods mainly transfer supervision to upstream scoring models and leave fusion modules jointly unoptimized. We propose UniRec, a Unified Cross-stage Recommendation Fusion framework that jointly optimizes pre-ranking and ranking fusion agents. UniRec employs a coupled dual-agent architecture with partially shared embeddings and stage-specific fusion functions. It further introduces Dual-Axis Preference Optimization to combine stage-local preferences with downstream-to-upstream preference transfer. Attribute Group-Relative Regularization (AGRR) mitigates reward-induced distribution drift by normalizing preference advantages within attribute groups. To improve efficiency, Compact Pairwise Preference Aggregation (CPPA) reduces the objective-dependent pairwise complexity, while Confidence-Aware Pair Pruning (CAPP) further reduces the evaluated pair space. Extensive offline and online experiments on a production short-video system demonstrate consistent gains over single-stage fusion and cross-stage coordination baselines. In a nine-week online A/B test, UniRec improves total watch time by $0.675\%$ and app usage time by $0.616\%$, and has been fully deployed in production.
♻ ☆ EKLAV: Elicited Key CoT Learning via Answer only superVision
Adarsh Singh, Aman Singh, Kushal Raj Bhandari, Soham Dan, Anoop Kumar, Vivek Gupta
Reasoning distillation trains a student to reproduce both the teacher's chain-of-thought trace and its final answer. We ask whether the trace is better used as privileged training context than as an imitation target. EKLAV keeps the teacher's reasoning in the input sequence but supervises only the final task answer, applying a task-dependent placement that moves part or all of the trace into the prompt. On BRIGHT passage reranking, EKLAV improves average nDCG@10 at all four tested checkpoints across two model families, winning 41 of 48 model-domain comparisons while reducing training compute by up to 31.6% and inference time by up to 32.7%. On four held-out table-reranking benchmarks, it is the best of four conditions on three, exceeding full-trace distillation by 3.0 points and answer-only training without reasoning by 5.5 points on average. Analysis of generated traces reveals that EKLAV students defer their first verbalized verdict later (0.76 vs. 0.44 relative position), reverse fewer decisions (5% vs. 16%), and produce reasoning more predictive of their own rankings than STD-COT's, though less predictive than the base model's. The recipe reuses a fixed teacher corpus, requires no student rollouts or iterative teacher feedback, and applies to both pointwise and listwise formulations. Code and Data are at https://github.com/AdarshSingh7647/Eklavya
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures
♻ ☆ HEM-Med: A Hierarchical Agentic Memory Framework for Safe Multi-Center Medication Recommendation
Min Xiao, Jin Li, Shoujin Wang, Yeguang Zhen, Yishuo Li, Wenpeng Lu
Medication recommendation (MR) is critical for clinical decision support. While existing MR methods are mostly designed for single-center learning, where only one independent hospital is involved, multi-center MR with hospitals of different scales has become increasingly demanding in practice. In multi center settings, abundant data from large medical centers can improve recommendation performance for low-resource centers. Despite a few preliminary attempts on this task, two critical gaps remain. Gap 1: Existing multi-center methods fail to disentangle transferable cross-hospital clinical experience from hospital-specific prescribing patterns, limiting clinical feasibility and physician acceptance. Gap 2: They commonly overlook multi label safety constraints of MR, including drug-drug interaction risks and local formulary feasibility, which are essential for safe real-world deployment. To address these gaps, we propose HEM-Med, a novel hierarchical agentic memory framework for multi-center MR. To address Gap 1, we design a disentangled hierarchical memory module that builds patient-level medication context attribution records and disentangles them into cross hospital experience memory and hospital-specific residual memory. To address Gap 2, we introduce a safety-aware medication set generation module, which integrates dual-level experience retrieval with safety-aware set decoding to produce clinically relevant, safer, and locally adaptive medication recommendations. Experiments on a real-world multi-center eICU dataset show that HEM-Med outperforms representative transfer learning, LLM-based, and MR baselines in terms of both recommendation accuracy and safety.
comment: BIBM 2026
♻ ☆ RIT-RAG: Navigating Document Corpora with Retrieval-Induced Trees
Meghanadh Pulivarthi, Swaraj Kumar Biswal, Kushagra Bhushan, Yatin Nandwani, Sachindra Joshi, Dinesh Raghu
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) grounds language models in external corpora. Agentic RAG enables iterative search, yet exposes the model to isolated chunks without document structure, making it difficult to distinguish relevant evidence from chunks that merely resemble the query. Structure-aware methods such as PageIndex navigate using the structure but cannot scale to structures of large corpora that cannot fit in the LLM context. Hence, they first commit to a single document using a document retriever and cannot recover from a wrong choice. We propose RIT-RAG (Retrieval-Induced Tree RAG), which combines content retrieval with structural navigation. Offline, RIT-RAG builds a tree for each document from its table of contents or sitemap. At query time, it retrieves a broad set of chunks and uses their positions to induce manageable sub-trees, potentially across multiple documents. An LLM agent navigate these sub-trees, selectively reads promising nodes, and reformulates queries when needed. Thus, retrieval proposes where to look, while the agent decides what to read. Across financial, scientific, and customer-support benchmarks, RIT-RAG achieves the highest answer accuracy among vanilla, graph-based, and agentic baselines. On EntQABench, our new benchmark of 2.84 million technical-documentation webpages, it improves accuracy by 6.6--11.4 points over the strongest baseline across three LLMs.
♻ ☆ Advertising to Agents: Measuring Description-Framing Bias in LLM Tool Selection NeurIPS 2026
Haochuan Kevin Wang
AI agents often pick tools from registries, where each provider writes its tool's description; we ask whether sales language there changes which tool an agent picks. We built pairs of listings that differ in one way (praise, a verifiable specification, or list order) and asked two OpenAI models to call one tool. In a preregistered study, stacked praise (four kinds) raised a tool's pick rate by about 43 percentage points, matching or beating a verifiable specification. Praise also pulled some picks toward tools whose numeric limit was too small. With identical listings, the first-listed tool was picked about 72 points more often. Structured fields helped agents pick the capable tool; sales text beside them reduced or erased that gain. An exploratory study of five models shows the same direction; a "Sponsored" label dampened it, and a system-prompt warning moved one model. Registries could list limits as fields, hide sales text from agents, and randomize order. Stacked praise replicated on held-out domains; no single kind did after correcting for multiple tests. Preregistered results are provisional until blind phrase ratings are complete, and cover two small models.
comment: 27 pages (9-page main text), 7 figures, 29 tables. Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop "The Agentic Web: Networked, Continually-Adapting Agent Ecosystems"
Logic in Computer Science
☆ SparseMax-dSTL: Sound Robustness with Horizon-Independent Gradient Allocation for Temporal Logic Trajectory Optimization
Sai Sandeep Damera, Ryan Matheu, John S. Baras, Calin Belta
A gradient-based solver that enforces a Signal Temporal Logic (STL) specification uses a smooth approximation of its quantitative semantics, the robustness. In safety-critical trajectory optimization, this approximation must have two properties. First, it must be sound, that is, nonnegative only on trajectories that satisfy the specification. Second, at each temporal operator, the weight of its gradient on the violating samples must stay bounded away from zero, however long the horizon. The approximations in use, including the log-sum-exp, its sound variant, and the generalized-mean robustness, do not have both. We introduce lower approximations of the minimum and the maximum whose gradients are sparsemax projections, and we prove that the robustness built from them has both. It lies below the exact robustness and is therefore sound, and its error has a bound that is independent of the number of samples and known before optimization. The gradient of each approximation is exactly zero on every sample beyond a data-dependent threshold, so the weight on violating samples a gap beyond the others has a positive lower bound at every horizon. On a planar unicycle and on a seven-joint manipulator beside a person in simulation, the log-sum-exp approximation is positive on a violating trajectory. As the horizon of the manipulator's task grows from 10 to 80 s, the gradient weight of the sound variant on the violating samples falls from 0.22 to 0.04, while that of sparsemax stays at 1. In a constrained trajectory optimization of the unicycle, the constraint on the log-sum-exp robustness returns a violating trajectory, whereas the constraint on the sparsemax robustness returns a trajectory that satisfies the specification with the required margin.
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
☆ A generalised and modular proof-theoretic semantics for sequent systems
Victor Barroso-Nascimento, Arghya Chakrabarty, Elaine Pimentel
Base-extension semantics explains logical consequence via derivability in atomic systems. Extending this approach across logics requires careful control of structural principles and contexts. We present a modular sequent-based framework in which support is indexed by multisets of atomic resources and the semantic clauses for connectives are guided by their left introduction rules. The framework separates additive from multiplicative behaviour and makes explicit the contributions of structural rules and restrictions on sequents. We establish soundness and completeness for classical and intuitionistic propositional logic and for multiplicative-additive fragments of classical and intuitionistic linear logic. We then investigate axiomatic extensions of intuitionistic logic through Jankov logic. Two classes of atomic bases yield sound and complete semantics. Completeness is proven using two novel and modular methods using simulation bases, one of which is constructive. These results provide a common semantic treatment of several logical systems while identifying the additional conditions needed to extend the framework beyond structural variations.
☆ LLM-Assisted Bi-Approximate CHC Solving
Baiting Jiang
Constrained Horn clause (CHC) solvers often struggle to discover deep counterexamples whose derivations may require extensive rule unfolding. Although large language models (LLMs) can propose long-range symbolic relations, prior work on formally checked LLM-assisted verification has mainly focused on generating inductive invariants and concrete traces. We exploit this broader capability through Derivation Power Under-approximations (DPUs). Each DPU is a solver-certified under-approximation of the relation induced by a multi-step CHC derivation. An LLM proposes each DPU with symbolic intermediate-state witnesses that enable SMT validation without introducing additional quantifiers. Validated DPUs can be composed and reused soundly. Building on this mechanism, our LLM-assisted framework HornCraft combines invariant generation for over-approximation with DPU generation for under-approximation in CHC solving. On 260 linear and nonlinear integer-arithmetic CHC-COMP benchmarks left unresolved by a 30-minute Spacer run, HornCraft returns certified verdicts for 228 instances. It certifies 42 instances as unsafe, compared with 22 when DPU construction and reuse are disabled.
comment: 22 pages, 8 figures, 5 tables
☆ LogicVal:A Logic-Formalized Benchmark for Constraint Satisfaction in Text-to-Image Generation
Savitha Sam Abraham, Marjan Alirezaie, Hossein Rahnama
Text-to-Image (T2I) generative models have made significant progress in producing high-fidelity images from natural-language prompts. Alongside this progress, numerous benchmarks have been developed to evaluate capabilities such as attribute binding, numeracy, spatial reasoning, and commonsense reasoning. In this work, we propose a new perspective on T2I evaluation by casting it as a constraint-satisfaction problem. We introduce a logical framework that formally specifies the benchmark domain, including objects, attributes, and relations, alongside the constraints that generated images must satisfy. We evaluated four state-of-the-art T2I models across 9 classes of constraints ranging from a single-object-attribute to multi-object relationships constraints involving logical operators ($\forall, \exists, count, \rightarrow$). Our results reveal a substantial gap between single-object and complex conditional multi-object relationship constraint classes, with the best-performing model achieving 98% accuracy on the former and just 53% on the latter. We assess compositional generalisation, finding that the best-performing model`s accuracy drops from 84% on single-constraint prompts to 20% when satisfying multiple constraints simultaneously. Identifying unsatisfiable constraints is also challenging, with the best model correctly recognizing only 23% of such prompts. Building on this framework, we introduce \textbf{LogicVal}, an evaluation methodology that combines neural visual detection with logical reasoning to assess constraint satisfaction in generated images. On CLEVR, LogicVal achieves ROC-AUC scores ranging from 0.88 to 0.98, indicating strong alignment with human judgments. These findings underscore the value of logic-based evaluation for characterizing T2I model capabilities and limitations.
comment: Preprint. Under review. Savitha Sam Abraham and Marjan Alirezaie contributed equally
☆ Model Checking for Noisy Toric Words
Mihir Vahanwala
Toric words have recently gained attention as a means to model the behaviour of dynamical systems such as linear loops. This work is concerned with describing when the toric model is precise enough to decide whether the trace of a system is contained in an omega-regular language. Our contributions are threefold. (i) We use topological means to generalise a class of toric words by defining noise-robust dynamical systems and their sets of noisy traces. We prove that all noisy traces of a system are almost-periodic, and have the same set of recurrent factors. (ii) We apply the abstract techniques above to concrete sequences obtained as sign descriptions of real algebraic linear recurrence sequences (LRS), and show that the language-membership problem for sign descriptions of LRS with few dominant roots is decidable. (iii) We show that noisy traces of noise-robust dynamical systems are indistinguishable to a prefix-independent omega-regular language, and inclusion is decidable provided the common language of their recurrent factors is recursive. We incidentally obtain properties of prefix-independent omega-regular languages that may be of independent interest.
☆ Controlled PROP: Theory and Applications to Quantum Circuits
Noé Delorme, Simon Perdrix
Control is a fundamental concept in quantum and reversible computational models. It enables the conditional application of a transformation to a system, depending on the state of another system. We introduce a general framework for diagrammatic reasoning featuring control as a constructor. To this end, we provide an elementary axiomatization of control functors, extending the standard formalism of PROPs to controlled PROPs. As an application, we show that controlled PROPs facilitate diagrammatic reasoning for quantum circuits. In particular, they admit a simple and complete axiomatization involving at most three qubits, whereas in the standard PROP setting, completeness necessarily requires axioms involving arbitrarily many qubits.
♻ ☆ LeanPRM: Lean-Grounded Process Supervision for Natural Language Proof Verification
Rodney Lafuente-Mercado, Salman Rahman, Jingyan Shen, James Shiffer, Saadia Gabriel, Pavel Izmailov
AI systems now write long and difficult mathematical proofs, and checking their step-by-step validity is becoming a bottleneck. A learned verifier could check proofs cheaply, but training one requires a correctness label on every step, and such labels are hard to obtain for open-ended proofs. Existing methods take them from human annotators, which is costly, or derive them from final answers, which proofs do not have, and formalizing each proof in Lean requires expert effort. We introduce LeanPRM, a framework that uses the Lean proof assistant to create step-level labels for natural-language proofs. A model writes a natural-language proof together with a paired formal proof, without feedback from Lean. Lean then labels every step, and a second model discards failures caused only by the formal syntax, so that the negative labels mark errors in the mathematics. LeanPRM contains 10,634 proofs with 152K labeled steps and no human annotation. A Qwen3-4B verifier trained on LeanPRM raises exact step-label accuracy on a held-out set of 200 proofs (LeanPRM-Bench) from 48.2 to 74.7, as opposed to 60.3 when the same base model is trained on PRM800K. It also selects better proofs in best-of-N selection on IMO-level problems, and outperforms the PRM800K-trained verifier on three of four external verification benchmarks. Training on LeanPRM improves verifiers at every size from 0.6B to 8B parameters on LeanPRM-Bench, Hard2Verify and IMO-GradingBench. Given the labels need no human annotation, LeanPRM can grow with the supply of formal statements, offering a path to step-level feedback on AI-generated proofs that are hard for humans to check.
comment: 29 pages, 9 figures. Project page: https://rlafuente.com/lean-prm
♻ ☆ Synthesis of Infinite State Systems
Ohad Drucker, Alexander Rabinovich
The classical Church synthesis problem, solved by Buchi and Landweber, treats the synthesis of finite state systems. The synthesis of infinite state systems, on the other hand, has only been investigated few times since then, with no complete or systematic solution. We present a systematic study of the synthesis of infinite state systems. The main step involves the synthesis of MSO-definable parity games, which is, finding MSO-definable uniform memoryless winning strategies for these games.
♻ ☆ A Gradient-Optimized TSK Fuzzy Framework for Explainable Phishing Detection
Lohith Srikanth Pentapalli, Jon Salisbury, Josette Riep, Kelly Cohen
Phishing attacks represent an increasingly sophisticated and pervasive threat to individuals and organizations, causing significant financial losses, identity theft, and severe damage to institutional reputations. Existing phishing detection methods often struggle to simultaneously achieve high accuracy and explainability, either failing to detect novel attacks or operating as opaque black-box models. To address this critical gap, we propose a novel phishing URL detection system based on a first-order Takagi-Sugeno-Kang (TSK) fuzzy inference model optimized through gradient-based techniques. Our approach intelligently combines the interpretability and human-like reasoning capabilities of fuzzy logic with the precision and adaptability provided by gradient optimization methods, specifically leveraging the Adam optimizer for efficient parameter tuning. Experiments conducted using a comprehensive dataset of over 235,000 URLs demonstrate rapid convergence, exceptional predictive performance (accuracy averaging 99.95% across 5 cross-validation folds, with a perfect AUC i.e. 1.00). Furthermore, optimized fuzzy rules and membership functions improve interoperability, clearly indicating how the model makes decisions - an essential feature for cybersecurity applications. This high-performance, transparent, and interpretable phishing detection framework significantly advances current cybersecurity defenses, providing practitioners with accurate and explainable decision-making tools.

Social and Information Networks
☆ Source Attribution and Audience Uptake in Digital Witnessing: Evidence from a Chinese Diaspora Account on X
Huiqian Lai, Runze Ding
Digital-witnessing research explains how citizen testimony becomes publicly visible. Less is known about audience uptake after publication and whether the attributed source corresponds to the form of response. This study analyzes 47,635 posts (April 2022 to May 2026) from Teacher Li Is Not Your Teacher, a diaspora-based account that curates and publishes reports and testimony from inside China for transnational audiences. Among 25,093 witness-relevant posts, 3,601 explicitly attribute their material to ordinary submitters. These posts receive more replies than other witness-relevant posts across adjusted analyses and show a more reply-oriented profile. The primary doubly robust retweet estimate is near zero. Among audited replies to November 2022 user-submitted posts, 91.4% substantively engage the focal material. The pattern is consistent with ordinary-person source attribution presenting testimony as situated and open to public response. The study extends digital witnessing beyond visibility by separating redistribution from the public response that gathers around testimony.

☆ The Kemeny-Braess Paradox in Random Graphs
Manuel Bodirsky, Lorenzo Ciardo, Mihyun Kang
In 2016, Kirkland and Zeng initiated the mathematical treatment of Braess paradox for random walks on graphs using Kemeny's constant as the measure of travel time. We study this phenomenon for the Erdős-Rényi random graph $G(n,p)$. An edge in a connected graph is called Kemeny-Braess if its deletion preserves connectedness and decreases Kemeny's constant, while a nonedge is Kemeny-Braess if its insertion increases Kemeny's constant. Let $\bar d=(n-1)p$ be the expected degree of $G\sim G(n,p)$, and assume that $\bar d-\log n\to\infty$, so that $G$ is connected with high probability. We determine the sharp asymptotic thresholds for the existence of both types of paradoxical behaviour. With $C^*=1/(1-\log 2)$, the threshold for Kemeny-Braess edges is $\bar d=C^*\log n$, whereas the threshold for Kemeny-Braess nonedges is $\bar d=2C^*\log n$. Hence, as the expected degree $\bar d$ increases, the connected regime exhibits three phases: first Kemeny-Braess paradox occurs for both edges and nonedges, then only for nonedges, and finally it disappears. In particular, in the dense regime, with high probability $G$ has no Kemeny-Braess edges or nonedges. This contrasts sharply with the spectral gap of the normalised Laplacian, for which Braess' paradox persists at constant edge density. Our proof combines a spectral-moment expansion of Kemeny's constant with uniform edge-perturbation estimates. Near the thresholds, the sign of the perturbation is governed by the endpoint degrees, and binomial large deviations yield the constant $C^*$ and the factor of two between the two thresholds.
☆ Modeling Group Socialization in Online Communities
Vinay Koshy, Iris Zhong, Karrie Karahalios, Benjamin Mako Hill, Amy X. Zhang
Newcomers to online communities must learn a group's norms to participate successfully. This process is known as socialization, and has been the subject of considerable study in the online communities literature. Foundational work on group socialization in social psychology, however, suggests that socialization is actually a bidirectional process: individuals and communities adapt to each other's needs. In this work we develop a formal quantitative model of socialization, and present the first large scale empirical validation of the bidirectional socialization hypothesis using Reddit data. More specifically, we focus on linguistic socialization, and model users' comments in online communities as a mixture of in-group language and language from ``background'' communities they previously participated in. On a dataset of 112 subreddits (7.8 million tokens) find that our bidirectional model makes predictions that better generalize across users and time than two unidirectional socialization models. Furthermore, we conduct a qualitative analysis in which we demonstrate that our model is able to extract interpretable socialization patterns from the data that align with the existing literature. Specifically our model is able to learn that users conform more to group norms in topically niche communities with stricter content moderation rules, and that long time users conform more than newcomers. We emphasize that the claims made in this paper are explicitly falsifiable -- we are staking out a clear claim about what the socialization process looks like, and encourage future work to challenge our model.
☆ Location, Location, Generation: Where You Ask Matters for Generative Engine Optimization
Mahe Chen, Nick Koudas
Generative search engines answer local and commercial questions with a written answer and a few cited sources. A growing practice of generative engine optimization (GEO) monitors which sources and brands these answers show, typically from a single place. In this paper, we present a controlled audit of how the user's location changes the sources that generative engines cite. We ask 300 questions of ChatGPT with 19 declared locations, and of ChatGPT and Gemini from five network locations, each twice to measure run-to-run noise (31,200 answers). The engines take location from different channels. ChatGPT follows the location an application declares, down to the city: it writes the place into its own searches, and its search backend localizes results even when the queries name no place. It ignores the network. Gemini ignores the declared location and follows the country of the network, changing most of its sources even for questions that do not depend on place. The businesses the answers recommend change with the sources. Thus, visibility in generative search is specific to the user's location, and audits must control both channels.

☆ Bridging the Language Gap in Scholarly Data II: Enhancing Gender Inference for Chinese Names
Lisette Espín-Noboa, Mingrong She, Ana Maria Jaramillo, Liuhuaying Yang
Perceived gender inference from names is important for inclusive scientometrics research, yet existing methods perform poorly on non-Western scholars. We address this gap for Chinese names, which appear in two forms, Hanzi and Pinyin, its Romanized form (e.g., Zhang Wei, Li Na). In international bibliographic records, names are often available only in Pinyin. However, a single pinyin name can correspond to multiple distinct hanzi characters with different gender associations, so gender inference from Pinyin alone is intrinsically ambiguous. To address this, we first develop two hanzi models, a regression model that produces a continuous gender score from 0 (male) to 1 (female), and a classification model that outputs one of three labels (\em{male}, \em{neutral}, \em{female}). We train them on a sample of hanzi names from Chinese-language physics publications, rated by 11 native Chinese speakers. On this sample, the models achieve an RMSE of $0.09$ and an R$^2$ of $0.85$ (regression), and macro-AUC of $0.97$ and a Cohen's $κ$ of $0.81$ (classification), demonstrating high performance that is robust to class imbalance. For pinyin names, we propose a pipeline that aggregates hanzi predictions via transliteration and frequency weighting, together with an ambiguity score that flags names whose gender cannot be resolved from Pinyin alone. Benchmarked against three off-the-shelf tools (Namsor, GPT, and Claude), our models achieve the highest agreement with human annotations for both gender scores and gender labels, in both scripts. Applied to an independent sample of Chinese-named authors in APS journals, our models assign a gender to every name, whereas existing Pinyin-based methods leave between 20\% and 100\% of names unclassified. These findings demonstrate the importance of hanzi-level information for reliable gender inference of Chinese names. Code and data are publicly available.

☆ What Remains Without Test Labels? Re-evaluating a Graph-Level Anomaly Detection Benchmark
Yujie Lu, Da Yan
Graph-level anomaly detectors are trained only on normal graphs, yet benchmarks may use test labels for model selection. We examine whether UB-GOLD results reused by later papers support label-free detection. We audit UB-GOLD and 14 GLAD code bases, re-run 21 detectors on UB-GOLD's folds under selection rules with and without test labels, and evaluate sensitivity to known structural changes. Test labels select checkpoints in UB-GOLD's shared training loop and checkpoints or hyperparameters in 8 of the 14 code bases. UB-GOLD also evaluates its kernel baselines against misaligned labels. Across nine datasets, selecting checkpoints by test AUROC adds an average of 5.12 AUROC points [3.97, 6.24] for the 12 UB-GOLD detectors relative to the final checkpoint and 4.13 [3.32, 4.79] relative to held-out normal graphs. In a post hoc permutation analysis with no truly better checkpoint, picking the best of noisy test evaluations still yields a gain more than half as large as the one observed against the final checkpoint. Configurations tuned on test labels score a further 1.53 points [0.64, 2.42] above repository defaults, a gap that mixes the value of test labels with that of tuning itself. With tuned hyperparameters and label-free checkpoint selection, the two strongest detectors retain their lead, while comparisons below them are less stable. Six of eight detectors evaluated out of sample miss size-preserving composition changes that graphlet counts detect. We recommend reporting results selected without test labels as the main comparisons and release per-run outputs that allow verification without retraining.

☆ Graphlet-based Decentralized Finance Transaction Method Classification
Célestin Coquidé, Alessio Brini, Natkamon Tovanich
Decentralized Finance (DeFi) transactions involve complex interactions among accounts, smart contracts, and tokens. We investigate whether network topology can identify transaction methods that describe DeFi operations. We extract directed graphlet features to classify the 30 most frequent methods. Our results show that graphlet features complement event log counts in improving classification performance. Using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), we further derive model explanations that reveal method-specific graphlet structural patterns.

☆ "You" Is Not Toxic: How LLM Labelers Rewrite the Web's Conversation Laws
Liang Yue, Eric A. Vance
What the Web community believes about toxic conversations, such as that toxicity rises in longer and deeper threads, was measured mostly with Google's Perspective API, which is shutting down; large language models (LLMs) will make the next measurements. We find that LLM labelers mistake second-person address for toxicity, and that this one bias manufactures laws that human labels do not show. On 1.25 million news comments with crowd labels, Claude Haiku flags 12% of the non-toxic comments that contain no "you" and 51% of those with four or more; a single crowd rater flags 6% and 10%. Deeper replies address someone more often, so under Haiku toxicity rises with reply depth (+0.93 percentage points per level), while under the crowd's labels it slightly declines (-0.12). Rewriting "you" in the third person removes two thirds of the false rise; flagging only as many comments as the crowd does not remove it, and showing Haiku the parent comment enlarges it. All seven LLMs we test over-flag "you", and at the crowd's flag rate, without the parent, any false rise of the open ones vanishes at a fixed number of second-person words; Haiku also over-flags "you" on Reddit, Gab and Wikipedia talk pages. Agreement with human labels does not reveal the bias: we prove that a fixed Cohen's kappa leaves a law nearly unconstrained. We therefore certify the law instead of the labeler. Threadsafe uses the labeler's scores to choose which comments human raters label and to predict the others, and corrects the predictions with the human labels; linear laws are estimated without bias whatever the labeler does. In simulated audits its intervals for the laws keep nominal coverage from 250 labels on, where uniform-sample methods such as PPI++ fall short, and at 1,000 to 8,000 labels are 0.75 times as wide as those of design-based supervised learning (DSL); a thousand human labels rule out Haiku's rising law.

☆ Validating LLM-generated political networks with survey-reported partisan exposure
Marco Tonin, Michele Tizzoni, Bruno Lepri, Luca Maria Aiello
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate human behavior in social science research, including decisions, interactions, and social relationships. However, in network formation tasks, existing evaluations often focus on aggregate network properties, while networks with plausible structural properties may still fail to reproduce individuals' social and political environments. Here, we generate LLM-based political networks using personas sampled from the nationally representative ANES 2020--2022 Social Media Study and use respondents' survey-reported partisan exposure as an empirical benchmark for the political environments generated for the corresponding personas. We first characterize the structural properties and political assortativity of the generated networks, and then compare ego-level partisan exposure with the survey. We find that the structure and political assortativity of the generated networks vary across experimental configurations. More importantly, when comparing generated partisan exposure with the survey, some models generate stronger separation between Democratic and Republican egos than reported in the survey, with higher same-party and lower cross-party exposure, while others mainly underestimate Republican exposure across ego groups. Moreover, networks with similar political assortativity can still generate different partisan environments around the same personas, including among networks with plausible structural properties. Finally, generated networks show group-specific errors, under- or overestimating exposure to either Democrats or Republicans for specific social groups. These findings show that evaluating LLM-based social simulations only through aggregate outcomes can hide errors in the local environments through which those outcomes emerge, highlighting the importance of validation at both aggregate and individual levels.
♻ ☆ Accelerating Spanning-Centrality Approximation with Sampling-Aware Vectorized Random Walks
Gökhan Göktürk, Kamer Kaya
Spanning centrality quantifies an edge's importance through its share of a graph's spanning trees, and approximating it for all edges (AESC) requires processing large volumes of irregular random walks under a prescribed error bound. Its applications include phylogenetic analysis and network robustness assessment. We focus on this random-walk processing bottleneck and propose Sampling-Aware Bouquet Arrangement (SABA), a CPU sampling and scheduling scheme that orders walks initialized on a uniform grid so that adjacent walks execute together in SIMD-width groups, called bouquets. For fixed per-walk random inputs, the ordering preserves the multiset of sampled walks while improving locality during neighbor access. On synthetic benchmarks, SABA achieves geometric-mean speedups of 6.95x and 7.41x over traditional random-walk generation for 2,048 and 16,384 walks per vertex, respectively, and up to approximately 49x in the latter setting. Within AESC, the complete 16-thread SABA implementation is 58.23x faster than the original single-threaded TGT+ implementation on average.
♻ ☆ Bonsai: A class of effective methods for independent sampling of graph partitions
Jeanne Clelland, Kristopher Tapp
We develop effective methods for constructing an ensemble of district plans via independent sampling from a reasonable probability distribution on the space of graph partitions. We compare the performance of our algorithms to that of standard Markov Chain based algorithms in the context of grid graphs and state congressional and legislative maps. For the case of perfect population balance between districts, we provide an explicit description of the distribution from which our method samples.
♻ ☆ A null model to detect coordinated online behavior integrating evidence from multiple indicators
Filipi Nascimento Silva, Manita Pote, Lake Yin, David Axelrod, Ashwin Balasubramanian, Luca Luceri, Filippo Menczer, Alessandro Flammini
Coordinated online accounts can amplify messages and manipulate attention, but detecting such behavior is challenging due to confounding factors like account activity and item popularity. We propose a statistical null-model framework that assesses behavioral similarity between accounts by comparing observed coordination indicators against activity- and popularity-conditioned reference distributions. By combining evidence across multiple indicators and partners, our method can identify suspicious coordination links more accurately. Evaluations on nine labeled information-operation datasets involving over 152 thousand accounts show that aggregating p-values multiplicatively across indicators and partners yields improved detection performance. While results vary across information operations, this approach offers a generalizable and statistically principled tool for uncovering coordinated online behavior.

♻ ☆ GARG-AML against Smurfing: A Scalable and Interpretable Graph-Based Framework for Anti-Money Laundering
Bruno Deprez, Bart Baesens, Tim Verdonck, Wouter Verbeke
Money laundering, a global problem estimated to account for 2%-5% of the global GDP, required regulators to enforce stringent rules on financial institutions to combat it. One prominent laundering method, called smurfing, relies on breaking up transactions into smaller amounts to evade detection. Given the complexity of laundering schemes, involving numerous transactions across multiple parties, network analytics is an important tool for anti-money laundering. However, recent advances in network analytics have leaned heavily on black-box network embedding methods, limiting their utility in businesses. To address the specific nature of smurfing and banks' operational requirements, this paper introduces GARG-AML, a novel graph-based method that quantifies smurfing risk through a single interpretable metric derived from the structure of the second-order transaction network. Unlike traditional methods, GARG-AML provides a balance between computational efficiency and transparency, enabling integration into existing AML workflows. We demonstrate the scalability of GARG-AML on large random networks, and its performance on two open-source money laundering datasets. Our results highlight the potential of GARG-AML to enhance smurfing detection and support investigative decision-making.

♻ ☆ Faster Deterministic Integer Root Finding for Integer Polynomials
Itamar Nir
We give a deterministic algorithm for finding all integer roots of a square-free polynomial $f\in\mathbb Z[x]$ of degree $n$ with $\lVert f\rVert_\infty<2^b$. The running time is $$ \tilde{O}(n^{3/2}b), $$ improving the $\tilde{O}(n^2b)$ bound of Harvey and Hittmeir (Research in Number Theory, 2022). The algorithm follows the classical $p$-adic framework: find roots modulo a prime $p$, lift them modulo a high power of $p$, and verify the lifted candidates. The main new idea is to avoid searching for a prime for which $f\bmod p$ is square-free. Instead, we find a prime for which the total multiplicity of repeated roots modulo $p$ is small. This requires lifting repeated roots, which we handle using a weighted lifting tree. We also give a faster deterministic candidate-verification algorithm: given $n$ candidate integers smaller in absolute value than $2^b$, we decide which are roots of $f$ in $$ \tilde{O}(nb+\min(n^2,nb^2)) $$ bit operations. Together, these ingredients give the first deterministic subquadratic-in-$n$ improvement for integer root finding in the square-free case.
comment: 48 pages, 3 figures. An extended abstract will appear in SODA 2027
♻ ☆ Compiling Expert Procedures into Verified Programs: When a Small Model Is Enough
Vishvesh Bhat, Asad Aali, Muhammad Ahmed Mohsin
In procedural tool-use domains, how much of the gap between base models is procedure rather than capability? We build an explicit program from a teacher's traces and run it in front of unchanged small models, including an 8B model. The construction, PLVR , takes the reasoning traces of a teacher, Kimi-K3, clusters their segments to locate recurring operations, has a frontier model author one typed primitive per operation, each run by a small frozen model and assembles the program by A* search over a mined rule library, under a reference-action objective. At inference the program takes one of two forms: for troubleshooting and tool search it produces the chain of thought the student would otherwise generate for itself, and the student acts on it; for multi-turn tool matching the student proposes each action and the program checks, repairs, or retries it before it goes out. On the official tau2-Bench Retail and Telecom test sets and on LiveMCPBench, with three Nemotron base models and the same program for each, the answer depends on the domain. On Telecom, Granite-4.2-8B as the student goes from 43.0% to 91.2% under the program, and every Nemotron student reaches 93.3-94.4%, against at most 58.2% for fine-tuning on the same traces, prompt optimisation of the student, or two token-matched baselines. With Granite-4.2-8B as the student, the program is within 2 to 3 points of the Nemotron students on Telecom and within 3 on Retail, and 3 to 13 points below them on LiveMCPBench: where the domain is procedural an 8B student is enough, and on tool search the student still matters. On Retail and LiveMCPBench the program is competitive with the best baseline. The spread between base models shrinks from about 7 points to about 2, averaged over the suites, with no weights changed.
♻ ☆ Sparse Polynomial GCD Cannot Be Computed in Fixed-output Polynomial Time
Yichuan Cao, Ruyong Feng, Xiao-Shan Gao, Qiao-Long Huang, Ruichen Qiu
This paper shows that, assuming $\mathsf{P}\ne\mathsf{NP}$, sparse univariate polynomial GCD cannot be computed in fixed-output polynomial time over any fixed computable field. Precisely, there is no deterministic algorithm that can compute the GCD of sparse univariate polynomials over any fixed computable field with total bit complexity polynomial in the input size, with the output size as a fixed parameter. In particular, there is no deterministic algorithm for sparse polynomial GCD that runs in polynomial time with respect to both the input and the output sizes. This settles the open problem posed as Challenge 5 in the sparsity challenges. Furthermore, we show that the Roots of Unity Detection problem over finite fields is NP-hard under random reductions; that is, determining whether the GCD of a sparse univariate polynomial and $x^n - 1$ has nonzero degree is NP-hard.
